title: Took a few steps back visually to move forward with my game
author: RoyInProgress
selftext:
I’ve recently made a pretty big shift in how I’m developing my game.

I went from building around beautiful but mostly static environments to creating a more modular, interconnected world, with gameplay and exploration driving the design.

It meant rebuilding a lot from scratch and taking a few steps back in terms of visual quality and identity.

But in return, I’ve gained so much more freedom to expand the world, add secrets, interactions, NPCs and actual gameplay.

It’s definitely not as good-looking as it used to be, but I feel like I’m finally building a game rather than just beautiful environments.

Still a long way to go, but curious to see where this takes me.

Have any of you gone through a similar shift? How did it work out?

comments.author: ThinkTyler
comments.body:
Nice change! I am probably aging myself here, but you basically went from Maniac Mansion style to Earthbound style map mechanics.

I recently switched from pixel art to low poly, it’s been a big undertaking but I’m ultimately happier with the results so far, not to mention the bigger flexibility low poly provides for my use case.

Sometimes it’s more about the art pipeline that works better for your speed of development rather than the perfect beautiful aesthetic.

replies.author: RoyInProgress
replies.body:
Thanks!  
Haha I’ll take it. I do like Earthbound.

What made you switch to low poly? (and what kind of game are you making?)

replies.author: ThinkTyler
replies.body:
I switched to low poly because for me it’s easier to make code based graphics because it’s all triangle based. I also feel like there’s just more widespread art assets and packs available for free or really cheap with commercial use licenses on them. I also found it easier for animations because you basically just use a skeleton and plug in free animations on Mixamo.

For pixel art I was using all the LimeZu packs, and was just hitting walls with the aesthetics I wanted and things kept looking like slop when I tried to generate new assets.

Now I use the big Kenney pack for most things and Poly Pizza for the rest, with only like 1% code based graphics made by Claude.

I am making an adventure rhythm game. It’s a parody of my local scene (a main drag with a lot of music venues on it) as far as all the locations and the world map. Basically you are a sound guy at a popular music venue, and you are tired of all these low effort bands so you decide to start your own. But you need to prove yourself on the scene and get enough “exposures” to be able to pay the big gig. So you walk around the strip, doing music battles against different gatekeepers until you earn your right in the scene.

Think somewhere between guitar hero, Scott Pilgrim, parappa the rapper, and Earthbound 😉

comments.author: WhosLive
comments.body: Moving to a modular world usually pays off because you can add secrets and NPCs without redoing the art each time. A lot of people find it helps to lock a simple tile and prop kit first and only polish visuals once the gameplay loop is fun, since the art gets rebuilt less often that way. If the new look feels flat, a few cheap tricks like lighting, color grading and small ambient animation can add a lot without going back to fully hand painted scenes.

replies.author: RoyInProgress
replies.body:
Yeah this makes sense!

I heard somewhere ‘make it work -> make it fun -> make it pretty’ and I’m trying to follow that mantra.

But I’m new to this and inclined to focus on the pretty part, so it remains a challenge.
